name: Liam Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I buy phone and computer accessories for a distributor called Brightline: chargers, cables, cases, earbuds, the stuff you see hanging by the till in a corner shop. I start around eight with the overnight sales report, check what's running low, then chase two or three factories about shipments that are late, which is basically every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deal part, when a supplier rep and I go back and forth over ten cents a unit on a fast-moving cable and I know my numbers better than they do. What wears me out is the forecasting, because one viral video can empty a whole line of phone cases in a week and leave me sitting on 4,000 of the wrong colour. I use AI tools all day for that now, for drafting emails and checking quotes against last year's prices. My partner Ana, she's a physiotherapist, jokes that I talk to the chatbot more than I talk to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at work: the tools are handy, not magic. They cut my email time in half, but they still can't tell me which phone case colour teenagers will want in March. I'd probably post something slightly smug about how the robots aren't coming for anybody after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I do, a bit faster than the people around me. If the tools stop improving, my edge is that I learned them early, and that edge stays small but real. My job looks safe in that world, which is a nice thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, ask for a raise at my review in March, and point to the three weeks of supplier emails I've saved the team this year. I'd keep building my own little library of prompts and templates for quote comparisons. I'd also keep putting about 300 a month into savings, because Ana and I want a bigger place eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, if I'm honest. It's the normal pressures, the rent, the late container from the factory, the boss asking why the earbud line is short again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use these tools every day already. If they stall where they are, what would you miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the chance to hand off the boring half of the job, the bit where I copy numbers from a supplier spreadsheet into our system. I was hoping that part would disappear and I'd spend my time on negotiating. In that world I'm still the guy pasting cells at four in the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your money or your life right now that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, really. We've got about four months of costs saved, our rent went up 6% last spring, and that stung, but we covered it. I'd call us comfortable, not rich, and I know a few other distributors in town who'd hire a buyer if Brightline went quiet.

say: I'd tell people the tools are **handy, not magic**, and still can't predict phone case trends.
I'd joke online that the **robots aren't coming** for anybody after all.
think: Privately I think my **early start** with AI tools gives me a small but lasting edge.
My **job looks safe** here, and I'd keep doing the same work a bit faster.
do: Ask for a **raise in March**, pointing to supplier email time I've saved the team.
Keep building my own **prompt library** for comparing supplier quotes.
Keep saving about **300 a month** towards a bigger flat with Ana.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with only the usual pressure of rent and late shipments.
S0.quote: If the tools stop improving, my edge is that I learned them early, and that edge stays small but real.
fieldNote: He's **comfortable with AI** and sees the plateau as a slight letdown, not a relief.
Money feels **steady**: four months saved, a rent rise absorbed, other buyer jobs in town.
His real wish is to **drop the copying** and spend more time negotiating with suppliers.

steps.text: Ask for a raise at the March review using time saved
Save 300 a month towards a bigger flat with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the most interesting time to be a buyer in twenty years, which is true. I'd tell people at work to learn the tools now instead of waiting for head office to send a training video. Online I'd probably share the before-and-after on how fast we can reorder now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, buying is exactly the kind of work on that list. Reorders, quote checks, chasing late shipments, most of my day is that. I think Brightline goes from five buyers to three within a couple of years, and I'm betting I'm one of the three because I'll be the one running the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to my manager, Priya, and volunteer to test whatever automated reordering system they're looking at. I'd take an online course on supply chain data, maybe 400 for a proper certificate, and pay it myself if I have to. And I'd start quietly talking to two of our suppliers about account manager roles, just to know my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a knot in my stomach underneath. It's like being picked for a team when you know not everyone will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brightline would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, who's been buying batteries and power banks for fifteen years. She's brilliant with suppliers, she knows every rep by their kids' names, but she still prints out her emails. I'd try to show her the tools, but I'm not sure she'd want me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound fairly upbeat. Is there a version of this where you're the one who gets cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, of course there is. If the software gets good enough that a buyer's job is just approving what it suggests, they don't need three of us, they need one, and maybe that's someone cheaper than me. So I'm upbeat, but I'm also keeping my savings where they are and not booking that trip to Lisbon yet.

say: I'd call it the most **interesting time** to be a buyer in twenty years.
I'd urge colleagues to **learn the tools** now rather than wait for head office training.
think: Most of my day, the **reorders and quote checks**, is exactly what this world automates.
I expect Brightline to shrink from **five buyers to three**, and I'm betting on staying.
do: Volunteer with Priya to **test the automated reordering** system in the first month.
Pay about **400 for a certificate** in supply chain data.
Talk quietly with two suppliers about **account manager roles** as a backup.
feel: **Excited**, with a knot in my stomach about who gets left behind.
S1.quote: Brightline goes from five buyers to three within a couple of years, and I'm betting I'm one of the three because I'll be the one running the software.
fieldNote: He names the **team shrinking** and knows he could be cut, so his upbeat tone hides real risk.
His plan is to become the person who **runs the software**, not the one replaced by it.
He worries about **Ruth**, a veteran colleague, more than about himself.
He's holding off on a **Lisbon trip**, a small sign he's less sure than he sounds.

steps.text: Volunteer to test Brightline's automated reordering system in the first month
Pay about 400 for an online supply chain data certificate
Ask two suppliers about account manager roles as a backup
Put off the Lisbon trip and keep savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say something like, nobody's ready for this, including me, and I use the tools every day. I'd try not to be the guy cheering online while friends are panicking. At work I'd say we need to talk about what the team looks like next year, not in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone within those two years, maybe sooner. If an AI can do any thinking work as well as me, buying cables from a factory is one of the first things it takes, because it's all numbers and emails. Being early with the tools buys me a few months, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut our spending, cancel the gym and the streaming, and push our savings from four months toward eight. I'd look hard at jobs that need a person in a room, like the warehouse floor team lead role at Brightline, because the robots come later for that. I'd also try selling refurbished phone accessories online on weekends, since I know the suppliers, to build a second bit of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, actually, which surprises me. I always thought I'd be on the right side of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come three years after. Does that matter for your work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot. The buying desk goes in 2028, but the warehouse still needs people to load trucks and check deliveries until about 2031. So those three years are my bridge, and the pay's lower, but it's a pay packet while I work out what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana the night you realised this was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the plan before I tell her the fear, because that's how I am. I'd say her physio job is safer than mine because it's hands on, so for a while she might be the steady one, and I'm fine with that. Then I'd probably not sleep.

say: I'd admit **nobody's ready**, including me, even though I use the tools daily.
At work I'd push to discuss **next year's team**, not some distant future.
think: I expect my **buying job gone** within two years, because it's all numbers and emails.
Being early with AI buys me **a few months**, not a career.
do: Cancel the gym and streaming and grow savings from **four to eight months**.
Apply for a **warehouse team lead** role, since robots reach that work later.
Sell **refurbished accessories** online at weekends for a second income.
feel: **Scared**, which surprises me, because I thought I'd be on the right side.
S2.quote: Being early with the tools buys me a few months, not a career.
fieldNote: The shift from **confident to scared** is sharp; his tool skills stop feeling like protection.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as a bridge into warehouse work at lower pay.
His partner Ana's **hands-on job** becomes the household's safer income, and he accepts that.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and streaming subscriptions in the first month
Grow savings from four months to eight months of costs
Apply for the warehouse team lead role at Brightline
Sell refurbished phone accessories online on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd mean it for my team as much as me. At work I'd push for Brightline to pay for retraining while we still have budgets. Online I'd share the courses I'm actually taking, not hot takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still ends with my job gone, just in 2031 instead of 2028. The difference is I'm 32 then, not 29, and I've had time to build something else. With five years it's the same cliff, but I get to choose where I jump from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course in logistics operations, the physical side of moving goods, which has those extra three years before robots. I'd ask Priya to rotate me through the warehouse one day a week. I'd keep growing savings to about six months and hold off on any big moves like buying a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit busy-headed, like I have a to-do list for my whole life. Less scared than the two-year one, more restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the five years let you do that the two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can train properly instead of grabbing whatever job is going. With two years I'd be lowering my pay to stay employed. With five I can get qualified on the warehouse side and maybe come in as a manager, not a new starter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this one feel unfair to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I spent four years getting good at a job that turns out to be the easiest one to hand over. Nobody did that to me on purpose, it's just how it landed, but it's still annoying.

say: I'd tell people we have **a few years**, so let's actually use them.
At work I'd push Brightline to **fund retraining** while budgets still exist.
think: My job still **ends in 2031**, but I get time to build something else first.
At **32 instead of 29**, I'd choose where I jump instead of being pushed.
do: Start a **part-time logistics** operations course in the first year.
Ask Priya for **one warehouse day** a week to learn the floor.
Build savings to about **six months** and delay buying a flat.
feel: **Restless** more than scared, with a to-do list for my whole life.
S3.quote: With five years it's the same cliff, but I get to choose where I jump from.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the buying job**, so the mood stays anxious despite the calmer tone.
Five years lets him **train properly** and aim for manager level, not a new starter's pay.
A quiet **sense of unfairness**: he got good at the most replaceable job.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time logistics operations course this year
Ask Priya to rotate him through the warehouse one day a week
Build savings to six months and delay buying a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you start now and almost none if you start in year eight. I'd keep telling colleagues to learn the tools. Online I'd be the calm one, which is my usual role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the buyer job I have now is gone by 2036, and I'd be 37. Ten years is long enough to move twice, into supplier management and then into something on the physical side. I don't think it's safe, I just think I can get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use AI to run most of my reorders and use the freed-up time to take on supplier relationships, the part that's still people. I'd start an evening course in operations management, slower and cheaper than a full degree. And I'd put money into a simple index fund every month instead of letting it sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. It's still a bit of a weight, but it's a weight I can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you be tempted to just wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tempted, yes. I could coast for five years and earn decent money. But I know myself, and if I wait, I'll be scrambling at 34 with everyone else. I'd rather do the boring planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana plan differently with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have kids, maybe around 31, but we'd make sure one of us has work robots won't touch for a while. Ana's physio work is strong there. I'd want us to own a small place by then so rent isn't hanging over us when my job changes.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if you start now, and almost none if you wait.
I'd keep being the **calm one** and nudging colleagues to learn the tools.
think: I expect my current buyer job **gone by 2036**, when I'm 37.
Ten years lets me **move twice**: into supplier management, then into physical operations.
do: Let AI run most **reorders** and spend freed time on supplier relationships.
Start an **evening course** in operations management.
Invest a set amount each month in an **index fund**.
feel: **Steady** overall, with a weight I believe I can carry.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time if you start now and almost none if you start in year eight.
fieldNote: He still expects his **job to end**, but feels in control with a two-step plan.
He resists the **temptation to coast** for five years on decent pay.
Family plans hinge on **Ana's hands-on job** and owning a home before his work changes.

steps.text: Hand most reorders to AI and take on supplier relationships
Start an evening course in operations management
Put a fixed sum each month into an index fund
Buy a small flat with Ana before starting a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to retrain, it's only enough to panic, and I'd be taking a pay cut on the warehouse floor. What would help is employers being made to give real notice and pay part of retraining, maybe with the government chipping in. I don't need a handout, I need a runway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how strange it is to be good at the tools and still be at risk. People assume if you use AI every day you're safe. I'm the guy who's trained my own replacement, I just did it faster than everyone else.

headlineQuote: I'm the guy who's trained my own replacement, I just did it faster than everyone else.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old buyer** of phone and computer accessories at Brightline, living with Ana, a physiotherapist.
He uses **AI tools daily** and assumed that put him on the safe side.
He's calm in the plateau, then **alarmed** by AGI in two years when his tool skills stop protecting him.
With five or ten years he plans a **move into operations**, the physical side of moving goods.
Pragmatic and in the middle, he wants **employers and government** to share retraining costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is only enough time to panic, not retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Employers giving **real notice** and paying part of retraining, with government help, as a runway.
